title: ticketToPr and the fan-out walls

story: Monday, 09:00. After sprint planning, four tickets are assigned to Nova, our ticket-to-PR agent, in the same minute: RH-1234, RH-1235, RH-1236 and RH-1240. Nova plans each one, and three of the plans then wait for their requesters, who are in meetings until lunch. One of them is on holiday until Thursday.

Picture the simplest workflow: claim a big VM when the ticket arrives and keep it until the PR is open. By 09:01 four full machines are running. By lunch they have spent hours doing nothing while people decide, and the one waiting for Thursday will run for three days. Now picture a busy Monday with forty tickets instead of four.
hook.question: How does one run hold a machine only while the machine is working, and how do we stop many runs from taking more machines than we planned?

read.h: Plan small, wait for free, build big
p: ticketToPr is the Temporal workflow for one Nova ticket, started with the ID nova:RH-1234 as you saw in the lesson about one run per ticket. Its shape follows the money. Planning only reads code, so it claims a lite VM, the smallest size, and releases it as soon as the plan is posted. Waiting for the requester costs nothing at all: condition() with a timeout is a durable timer inside Temporal, so no VM runs, no worker is busy, and a deploy of the orchestrator, our Temporal worker that runs every agent workflow, does not lose the wait. Only an approved plan claims a full VM for the build.

Every claim sits in a try block whose finally releases the VM. That is the rule that keeps the bill honest: an error, a Stop from a person or a cancelled run all leave through finally. The release is wrapped in CancellationScope.nonCancellable, because a cancelled workflow would otherwise cancel the release too, and a forgotten VM costs money every hour until the sweeper, a job that destroys leftover VMs every 15 minutes, finds it.

notes.text: Signals are how a click in Slack reaches this function. The Slack app lesson shows where they come from.
Each sandbox step first takes a slot (next section), then a VM.
In the full version a question from Nova loops here: the VM is parked after 10 idle minutes and woken when the answer comes.
waitForPerson adds a reminder and a deadline to the wait. It returns false when the ticket was handed back or a person pressed Stop, and run.stopped says which. The lesson about waiting covers it.

deeper.h: Go deeper: why the workflow can be plain TypeScript
p: A workflow function looks like ordinary async code, but Temporal records every step in a history and can replay the function to rebuild its state on any worker. That is why the code must be deterministic: no fetch, no Date.now() for decisions, no Node APIs. Everything that touches the world, from claiming a VM to posting the plan, is an activity, and the workflow only calls activities.

Because runs live for days, every deploy lands in the middle of some of them. A change to workflow code goes behind patched("<change-id>"), so old runs replay the old path and new runs take the new one, and a replay test in CI runs saved histories against the new code on every pull request.

read.h: A fixed number of slots per agent
p: Plan small fixes the waiting, but not the Monday morning. Forty tickets would still mean forty planning VMs at once. So each agent has a fixed number of slots, where a slot is permission to have one VM running: Nova has 3, the CI fixer (the routine that repairs a red main branch) 2, the security fixer 1. A fourth Nova step waits in line until a slot comes back.

The line is itself a workflow that never ends, slots:nova, and it talks to runs with signals. A signal is a message to a running workflow, and Temporal stores it, so the line survives restarts without a database or a lock. Runs send it a request signal with their workflow ID; it answers with slotGranted when fewer than three runs hold a slot, and a release signal gives the slot back. withSlot wraps a step in request and release, and the release sits in finally for the same reason the VM release does. The order matters: a run takes the slot before it claims the VM and gives it back after the VM is released, so a run waiting for a person holds neither.

notes.text: Starting values. They are a cost decision, not a technical limit, and can be raised one agent at a time.
Sleeps, without any polling, until someone waits and a slot is free.
The run that waited longest gets the slot: first come, first served.
A workflow that lives forever must restart its history now and then; continueAsNew carries the holders and the line along.

deeper.h: Go deeper: the other fan-out walls
p: Slots are one of several walls against agent storms, which are many agents doing work nobody needed. Each agent also has its own task queue, such as ai-agents-nova and ai-agents-cifix, served by its own workers, so a flood of one kind of work cannot take every worker. Only the orchestrator starts runs, through startRun, and the VM has no route to Temporal, so an agent can never start another agent.

The kill switch, which stops one agent at once, is a row per agent in the database of the broker, the service that holds our GitHub, Jira and Slack credentials. A local activity (a short activity that runs inside the workflow's own worker) reads it before every step, so a stopped agent ends cleanly at the next step boundary and keeps its branch, and startRun reads it too and refuses new starts. To stop every open run of one agent at once, a person signals stop to all of them with one temporal workflow signal command that selects runs by the Agent search attribute, a field Temporal can filter runs by.

Temporal requires a timeout on every activity call, and our rule says no clock may cut an agent's work. Both can be true because of what Temporal does when a timeout fires: it retries the activity. workInSandbox is written to re-attach to the harness that is still running on the VM, so its 7-day start-to-close timeout ends one attempt to follow the harness, never the harness itself. It is a safety net, not a work limit.

The timeout that does catch trouble is the heartbeat timeout. While the harness runs, the activity calls heartbeat() every few seconds; if two minutes pass with no heartbeat, the worker process running it has died, and Temporal starts a new attempt on a healthy worker, which re-attaches. A dead VM is a different problem with its own rule, and the next lesson is about it. All of these presets live in one file, policies.ts, so every workflow behaves the same way when something is slow.

notes.text: AWS calls retry from 1 second up to 1 minute, 10 times.
Jira, Slack and GitHub calls through the broker retry without an attempt limit, so a long outage never makes them stop trying.

lab.title: Four tickets, three slots
needs: The course repo at ~/Projects/ai-agents-course (the lab starts from the p7-4 lab's files)
lab.goal: Run a small ticketToPr on a real Temporal dev server and make four tickets share Nova's three VM slots, with no slot held while a plan waits for approval.

guess.q: Nova has 3 slots. Four tickets arrive at once, each plans for 20 seconds, then waits for approval. What does the line look like 30 seconds later?

options.text: Three tickets wait for approval holding their slots, and the fourth is still waiting for a slot
options.why: That happens only if the approval wait sits inside withSlot. A run gives its slot back as soon as its plan VM is released.

options.text: Three tickets wait for approval with no slot, and the fourth is planning in the slot that came back
options.why: The slot covers only the time a VM runs. Waiting for a person is free, so the fourth ticket moves in at once.

options.text: All four are planning, because Temporal starts every workflow it is given
options.why: Temporal starts all four runs, but each run waits for slotGranted before it claims a VM. Runs and machines are counted separately.

follow.say: Copy the p7-4 lab's files, because they already connect to Temporal and start a worker on the ai-agents-nova queue.
follow.do:
cp -r ~/Projects/ai-agents-course/labs/p7-4/start ~/academy-labs/g3-10 && cd ~/academy-labs/g3-10
rm triggers.mjs try-default.mjs start-run.mjs
sed -i '' "s/WorkflowType = 'ticketToPr' AND //" clean.mjs
npm install
follow.see:
added 150 packages, and audited 151 packages in 4s
found 0 vulnerabilities

follow.say: Replace workflows.mjs with ticketToPr and the slot line. withSlot does nothing yet, which is the bug you will see first.
Replace activities.mjs with pretend sandbox activities that print what a real VM would do and work for 20 seconds.
Add a script that assigns four tickets at once, and a board that shows the slot line and every open ticket.
Start Temporal in the first terminal and Nova's worker in the second, and leave both open.
follow.do:
temporal server start-dev
# second terminal:
cd ~/academy-labs/g3-10 && node worker.mjs
follow.see:
Temporal Server:      localhost:7233
Temporal UI:          http://localhost:8233
…
Nova's worker is listening on the ai-agents-nova queue. Leave this terminal open (Ctrl+C stops it).

follow.say: In the third terminal assign the four tickets and look at the board, because this is Monday morning without slots.
follow.do: cd ~/academy-labs/g3-10 && node tickets.mjs && sleep 4 && node board.mjs
follow.see:
assigned RH-1234 to Nova → run nova:RH-1234
…
slots:nova  holding 0 of 3: -   waiting: -
  nova:RH-1240   Planning
  nova:RH-1236   Planning
  nova:RH-1235   Planning
  nova:RH-1234   Planning
(the worker terminal says "claimed a lite VM" four times: four machines for three slots)

lab.build: Write withSlot in workflows.mjs, following the numbered comment above it: register a slotGranted handler, signal request with your own workflow ID to slots:<agent>, wait with condition() until granted, run fn, and in finally signal release inside CancellationScope.nonCancellable. Restart the worker (Ctrl+C, node worker.mjs), then run node clean.mjs && node tickets.mjs. The board should show three holders and one ticket waiting for a slot; 30 seconds later, three tickets awaiting approval with no slot and the fourth planning. Approve one plan with temporal workflow signal --workflow-id nova:RH-1234 --name decidePlan --input '"approve"' and watch it take a slot again for a full VM.
checks: Right after node tickets.mjs, the board says holding 3 of 3 and one ticket shows Waiting for a slot.
About 30 seconds later the board shows three tickets Awaiting approval and holding 1 of 3.
The worker terminal never shows a fourth "claimed a lite VM" before a "released" line.
After you approve RH-1234, the worker prints "claimed a full VM", and temporal workflow result --workflow-id nova:RH-1234 shows "PR open: draft PR #2512".
Every "claimed" line in the worker terminal has a matching "released" line.
lab.fix: Someone wanted builds to start the moment a plan is approved, so they moved the approval wait inside the plan's withSlot: "keep the slot, the build will need it anyway". Make the same change (put the condition() for the decision inside the plan step's withSlot), restart the worker and run node clean.mjs && node tickets.mjs. A minute later the board says holding 3 of 3 with three tickets Awaiting approval, and the fourth ticket waits for a slot that will not come back until somebody returns from holiday. Put the wait back outside the slot.
explain: Why does a run give its slot back while it waits for a person, and what would happen on a busy day if it did not?
Why does the release of the VM and of the slot sit in finally, inside a non-cancellable scope?
The build activity has a 7-day start-to-close timeout. Why does that never cut Nova's work, and what does catch a dead worker?
lab.done: Four tickets never hold more than three VMs, waiting plans hold no slot, RH-1234 ends with a draft PR, and you stopped the worker and the dev server with Ctrl+C.

check.q: Why does ticketToPr release the planning VM before it waits for approval, instead of keeping it for the build?

options.text: Because a plan and a build need different code on the VM
options.why: Both run the same harness on the same image. The reason is time and money, not software.

options.text: Because the wait can last days, and a durable timer costs nothing while a VM costs money every hour
options.why: Plan small, wait for free, build big: only an approved plan pays for a full VM.

options.text: Because Temporal cannot wait while an activity holds a VM
options.why: Temporal could wait; it would just keep the VM running and the slot taken for nothing.

check.q: Three Nova runs hold slots and a fourth asks. What does the fourth run do?

options.text: It waits inside condition() until slots:nova signals slotGranted, holding no VM
options.why: The line hands out slots in order, and a run claims its VM only after it has a slot.

options.text: It fails with an error, and the Jira poll starts it again a minute later
options.why: Nothing fails. The run simply waits in line, and waiting in Temporal costs nothing.

options.text: It claims a VM and waits for a slot before using it
options.why: That would spend money while waiting. The slot comes first, then the VM.

check.q: The build's activity has startToCloseTimeout: "7 days". A big ticket builds for 8 days. What happens on day 7?

options.text: The harness on the VM is killed and the work since the last checkpoint is lost
options.why: The timeout ends Temporal's attempt to follow the harness, not the harness. Nothing on the VM is touched.

options.text: The run fails and Nova posts that it ran out of time
options.why: No clock ends a run in our platform. The timeout leads to a retry, not a failure.

options.text: Temporal retries the activity, and the new attempt re-attaches to the harness still working on the same VM
options.why: That is why the timeout is a safety net. The heartbeat timeout is what notices a dead worker.

p: ticketToPr lives in ai-agents/orchestrator/src/workflows/ticket-to-pr.ts and runs on the ai-agents-nova queue; the slot lines run as slots:<agent> in the ai-agents namespace, and withSlot sits in workflows/slots.ts. In the final version each sandbox step also goes through runWithRecovery, which replaces a dead VM (lesson g3-11), and the waits go through waitForPerson (lesson g3-12).

The timeouts and retry policies are in orchestrator/src/policies.ts: act for long VM work with the AWS retry policy, peopleApis for Jira, Slack and GitHub calls through the broker. The kill switch is a row per agent in the broker's database, and its third part, bumping the agent's epoch at the gateway, kills every live run token of that agent at once.

tickets.why: ticketToPr: plan on lite, wait for the decision, build on full, questions, release in finally.
The fan-out walls: startRun, one queue per agent, the slots workflow and withSlot, the kill switch.
The SHORT and LONG presets, the retry policies, heartbeats, patched and the replay test.

words.plain: Permission for one run to have one VM running. Each agent has a fixed number.
The slots:<agent> workflow that hands out slots in order and takes them back.
Plan on a lite VM, release it, wait for approval with no VM, and claim a full VM only for an approved plan.
A scope whose code runs even when the workflow is cancelled, used for every release.
How long an activity may go without reporting that it is alive before Temporal tries again on another worker.

review.q: From memory: Nova's slot count, and the order of the four calls in one sandbox step (slot, VM, release VM, release slot).
review.a: 3 slots. withSlot takes a slot, acquireSandbox claims the VM, finally releaseSandbox, then withSlot's finally releases the slot.

review.q: A teammate wants the approval wait inside withSlot "so the build starts faster". What do you answer?
review.a: Then runs waiting for people hold slots, and with three such runs Nova stops working for everyone. The few seconds to get a slot after approval cost nothing.

review.q: Why does withSlot give the slot back in finally, inside a non-cancellable scope, just like the VM release?
review.a: A run can end with an error, a Stop or a cancellation. Without finally, or if the cancellation also cancelled the release signal, the slot would stay taken, and Nova would work with one slot less until someone noticed.

remember: Hold a machine only while it works, and hold a slot only while you hold a machine: waiting for people is free.
